title: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
summary: Why LLM decoding is memory bound, how a cheap drafter plus one target pass yields several tokens with exactly the target's distribution, the speedup math, and Medusa, EAGLE, n-gram and vLLM in practice.
outcomes: Explain why verifying several guessed tokens costs about one decode step at small batch size
Prove with numbers that min(1, p/q) acceptance plus residual resampling yields exactly the target distribution
Compute expected tokens per round and walltime speedup from alpha, gamma and the cost ratio c
Explain how Medusa heads, tree attention and EAGLE's feature-level drafter raise acceptance
Choose a drafting method and judge when speculation helps or hurts in a serving system

lessons.title: Why decoding is slow and why checking guesses is cheap

blocks.md: Recall from GPU and inference basics: generating text runs the model once per new token, and at small batch sizes each of those decode steps is limited by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic. Every step streams all the weights (and the KV cache) from GPU memory to produce a single token per sequence.

Chen et al. (DeepMind) put a number on this ceiling: since all parameters must pass through the chips once per step, *model size divided by total memory bandwidth* is a hard lower bound on time per token for plain autoregressive sampling. In their setup Chinchilla 70B on 16 TPU v4 chips took **14.1 ms per token**.

The key observation behind speculative decoding is about *scoring*, not generating. Given a prefix plus a short guessed continuation of $K$ tokens, one forward pass of the big model returns the next-token distribution at every one of those positions, exactly as it does during training or prefill. Chen et al. argue this costs about the same as producing one token when $K$ is small, because each part of the step stays memory bound:

- **Linear layers**: the weights are read once whether they multiply 1 or 5 token vectors.
- **Attention**: the dominant cost is reading the KV cache, which does not grow with $K$.
- **All-reduces** between chips: a handful of token activations is latency bound either way.

blocks.title: Five tokens: plain decoding vs one speculative round

scenes.caption: Plain decoding: five sequential target steps at 14.1 ms each (Chinchilla 70B timing from Chen et al.) give five tokens in 70.5 ms.
Speculative round: a small draft model (1.8 ms per token in Chen et al.) guesses 4 tokens in 7.2 ms. Nothing is output yet; these are only guesses.

One target pass scores all 4 guesses plus one extra position, assumed to cost one ordinary step (14.1 ms). The round ends at 21.3 ms and yields between 1 and 5 tokens. Simplified: real verification is slightly slower than one step.

If all 5 tokens are kept, that is 4.26 ms per token against 14.1 ms. If the first guess is wrong, the round still gives 1 token, at 21.3 ms instead of 14.1 ms. The payoff depends on how often guesses survive.

blocks.md: This is speculative execution, the CPU trick of doing work before you know it is needed, applied to language models. Two groups published it independently: Leviathan, Kalman and Matias at Google (**speculative decoding**, 2022) and Chen et al. at DeepMind (**speculative sampling**, 2023). We call the big model the **target** and the cheap guesser the **draft** model.

Why not simply use a smaller model? Because it changes the answers. Distillation and quantization trade quality for speed. Speculative decoding makes a stronger promise: the tokens you get are distributed **exactly** as if the target had generated them alone. The draft only decides how many target steps you can skip.

Decoding is slow because each step moves all the weights to produce one token. Checking $K$ guessed tokens in one target pass moves the weights once, so every accepted guess is a target step you did not pay for.

blocks.prompt: A draft guesses 4 tokens and the target rejects the very first one. How many tokens does that round output: 0, or at least 1?
blocks.reveal: At least 1. The verify pass already computed the target's own distribution at the first position, so on a rejection the algorithm samples a replacement token from it (lesson 3 shows exactly which distribution). A round therefore never produces fewer tokens than a plain decode step; the risk is only the wasted draft time.

blocks.question: Why can the target model score 5 guessed tokens in roughly the time it takes to generate 1 token at batch size 1?
options: The target skips attention for guessed tokens
Guessed tokens use a lower precision path
The GPU runs 5 separate copies of the model in parallel
At small batch the step is memory bound: weights and KV cache are read once either way, and 5 token vectors add little arithmetic
blocks.explain: The cost of a small-batch decode step is dominated by reading weights and KV cache from memory. Multiplying those weights by 5 vectors instead of 1 adds arithmetic the chip has to spare, so latency barely changes (Chen et al.'s argument for linear layers, attention and all-reduces).

blocks.question: Which claim about speculative decoding is correct?
options: It speeds up decoding by letting a smaller model answer the easy prompts
It trades a small amount of quality for latency, like quantization
It produces the same output distribution as the target model and only changes how many target passes are needed
It only works with greedy decoding
blocks.explain: Both original papers prove the sampled tokens follow the target's distribution for any draft. Quality is unchanged; speed depends on how well the draft guesses. Lesson 3 covers sampling, not just greedy.

lessons.title: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding

blocks.md: Start with greedy decoding (temperature 0), where the target always picks its most likely token. Then verification is just a comparison: a guessed token is correct if and only if it equals the target's argmax at that position. One round of the loop with lookahead $\gamma$ (Leviathan's name; Chen calls it $K$) goes like this:

1. **Draft**: run the draft model $\gamma$ times autoregressively to get guesses $x_1, \dots, x_\gamma$.
2. **Score**: run the target once on prefix plus all $\gamma$ guesses. Because attention is causal, position $i$ sees only the prefix and $x_1..x_{i-1}$, so the pass returns $\gamma + 1$ next-token distributions $p_1, \dots, p_{\gamma+1}$.
3. **Verify** left to right: keep guesses while they match the target; stop at the first mismatch.
4. **Fix up**: append the target's own token at the first mismatch, or if every guess matched, a **bonus** token from $p_{\gamma+1}$.

blocks.title: Two rounds of speculative decoding with gamma = 4

scenes.caption: The engine asks the draft for 4 guesses after the prefix 'the cat'. The draft runs 4 cheap sequential steps.
One target forward pass over prefix plus 4 guesses returns 5 distributions: one for each guess position and one extra after 'mat'.
Compare: 'sat' and 'on' match, 'a' does not. Keep 2 guesses, replace 'a' with the target's 'the', and drop 'mat'. Three tokens from one target pass.
Next round starts from the longer prefix. The draft's KV cache for rejected tokens is discarded, and the loop repeats.
All 4 guesses match, so the algorithm also takes the bonus token 'warm' from the fifth distribution: 5 tokens from one target pass, the maximum of gamma + 1.
The target pass gives its argmax at all 5 positions at once. Position 4 (the bonus slot) has no guess; it is only used if every guess survives.
Positions 0 and 1 match, so both guesses are accepted. They cost one draft step each and no extra target step.
Position 2 mismatches: 'a' is rejected and the target's 'the' is written instead. Everything after it, 'mat' and the target's 'floor', is thrown away because it was computed for the wrong prefix.

blocks.md: Two properties fall out of the structure. First, every round outputs **at least one** target token, so the number of sequential target passes can never exceed plain decoding. Second, a round outputs **at most** $\gamma + 1$ tokens. The cost you risk on a bad round is the $\gamma$ draft steps plus any slowdown of the wider verify pass.

The idea of checking several predicted tokens with one pass is older than both 2022 papers: Stern, Shazeer and Uszkoreit's blockwise parallel decoding (2018) did it for greedy decoding: predict several steps in parallel, then keep the longest prefix the scoring model validates. What Leviathan et al. and Chen et al. added is a verification rule that works for **sampling** at any temperature, which is the next lesson.

A common bug: after a rejection, keeping the target's distributions for later positions. Those were computed with the rejected guess in the context, so they condition on a token that is no longer in the output. Only the distribution at the first rejected position is valid.

blocks.question: A round with gamma = 5 finds the first mismatch at guess 4 (1-based). How many tokens does it append?
blocks.explain: Guesses 1 to 3 are accepted and the target's own token replaces guess 4, giving 4 tokens. Guess 5 and the bonus slot are discarded because they were computed after a rejected token.

blocks.question: Why does the target pass produce gamma + 1 distributions rather than gamma?
options: Causal attention gives a next-token distribution after every input token, including after the last guess, which supplies a bonus token when all guesses pass
One extra position is needed to check the prefix
The draft also returns one distribution that is reused
It is an implementation detail that is never used
blocks.explain: The forward pass over prefix plus gamma guesses outputs a distribution after each of them. The last one, after guess gamma, is a free target prediction used only when all guesses are accepted, raising the maximum to gamma + 1 tokens per round.

lessons.title: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution

blocks.md: With sampling, 'does the guess match' no longer makes sense: the target might have produced several tokens. We need a rule that accepts a guess $x$ drawn from the draft distribution $q$ in such a way that the final token is drawn from the target distribution $p$. Notation follows Leviathan et al.: $p$ is the target, $q$ the draft. (Chen et al. use the opposite letters, so read carefully when comparing.)

The rule is a modified rejection sampler. Sample $x \sim q$. Accept it with probability $\min(1, p(x)/q(x))$: always if the target likes $x$ at least as much as the draft does, otherwise in proportion. If rejected, sample a replacement from the **residual** distribution, the part of $p$ that the draft under-covers:

blocks.tex: P(\text{accept } x) = \min\!\left(1, \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right), \qquad p'(x) = \frac{\max(0,\, p(x) - q(x))}{\sum_{y} \max(0,\, p(y) - q(y))}
blocks.caption: Temperature, top-k and nucleus sampling are applied to both p and q first; the rule works on whatever adjusted distributions you sample from.

blocks.md: A concrete case on a 4-token vocabulary {the, a, cat, dog}. Target $p = (0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1)$, draft $q = (0.3, 0.4, 0.1, 0.2)$. The draft over-proposes 'a' and 'dog', so those are the only tokens that can be rejected, each with acceptance probability $0.5$. The draft under-proposes 'the' and 'cat', so the residual puts all its mass there.

blocks.title: Toy vocabulary: how acceptance plus residual rebuilds p

scenes.caption: Target distribution p, the one we must sample from: 0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1.
Draft distribution q: 0.3, 0.4, 0.1, 0.2. Cheap to sample but wrong. Acceptance probabilities min(1, p/q) are 1, 0.5, 1, 0.5.
Probability of proposing x AND accepting it: q(x) min(1, p/q) = min(p, q) = 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1. Total acceptance probability is 0.7.
Rejection happens with probability 0.3. The residual max(0, p - q) = (0.2, 0, 0.1, 0) also sums to 0.3, normalized to (2/3, 0, 1/3, 0). Mass contributed: 0.2, 0, 0.1, 0.
Accepted mass plus residual mass: 0.3 + 0.2, 0.2 + 0, 0.1 + 0.1, 0.1 + 0 = 0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1. Exactly p. A 200,000-sample simulation gives 0.501, 0.201, 0.199, 0.099.

Contrast a plausible wrong rule: accept only if q(x) is at most p(x), else resample from p. It outputs 0.6, 0.12, 0.22, 0.06, biased toward 'the'. Resampling from p instead of the residual double counts.

blocks.md: The general proof is the same two terms. The chance of outputting $x$ is the chance of proposing and accepting it, plus the chance of rejecting anything times the residual's probability of $x$. Since $\sum_y \max(0, p - q) = 1 - \sum_y \min(p, q)$, the normalizer cancels the rejection probability:

blocks.tex: P(X = x) = \underbrace{\min(p(x), q(x))}_{\text{accepted}} + \Big(1 - \sum_y \min(p, q)\Big)\frac{p(x) - \min(p(x), q(x))}{1 - \sum_y \min(p, q)} = p(x)
blocks.caption: Works for any q, however bad. A bad draft only lowers the acceptance probability, never the quality.

blocks.md: Leviathan et al. call this per-position acceptance probability $\beta = \sum_x \min(p(x), q(x))$ and its average over the text $\alpha = E[\beta]$, the **acceptance rate**. It is one minus the total variation distance between $p$ and $q$ (half the sum of $|p(x) - q(x)|$), so it is 1 when the models agree and 0 when their supports are disjoint. For our toy pair, $\beta = 0.7$.

blocks.prompt: Greedy decoding is the special case where p and q are one-hot. What does the acceptance rule reduce to?
blocks.reveal: With one-hot distributions, $p(x)/q(x)$ is 1 when the draft's token is the target's argmax and 0 otherwise, so the guess is accepted exactly when it matches. The residual $\max(0, p - q)$ is then one-hot on the target's argmax. That is the comparison rule from lesson 2, so greedy is not a separate algorithm.

blocks.title: Verifying the round 'sat on a mat' with sampling
blocks.code:
def verify(p, q, drafts, rand):
    # p[i], q[i]: target and draft distributions
    # at draft position i (dicts token to prob)
    out = []
    for i, x in enumerate(drafts):
        ratio = min(1.0, p[i][x] / q[i][x])
        if rand() < ratio:
            out.append(x)            # accept guess
            continue
        res = {t: max(0.0, p[i][t] - q[i].get(t, 0.0))
               for t in p[i]}
        z = sum(res.values())
        res = {t: v / z for t, v in res.items()}
        out.append(sample(res))      # fix-up token
        return out
    out.append(sample(p[len(drafts)]))  # bonus
    return out

scenes.caption: Guess 0 'sat': q = 0.6, p = 0.7. The target likes it more than the draft, so the ratio is clipped to 1 and it is always accepted.
Guess 1 'on': q = 0.8, p = 0.6, ratio 0.75. The uniform draw 0.42 is below 0.75, so it is accepted.
Guess 2 'a': q = 0.5, p = 0.2, ratio 0.4. The draw 0.81 exceeds 0.4: reject.
Residual at position 2. Over {the, a, my, his}: p = (0.6, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1), q = (0.3, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1), so max(0, p - q) = (0.3, 0, 0, 0). Normalized, 'the' has probability 1.
The fix-up token 'the' is appended and the round returns 3 tokens. 'mat' and the bonus distribution are never examined.

blocks.md: Speculative sampling is exact in math, not bit for bit. Chen et al. note samples match the target 'within hardware numerics': different batching, kernels and random number streams change floating point results, so a fixed seed will not reproduce plain decoding token for token.
Accept with $\min(1, p/q)$, on rejection sample from $\text{norm}(\max(0, p - q))$. Accepted mass is $\min(p, q)$ and residual mass is $p - \min(p, q)$; they add up to $p$ for any draft.

blocks.question: Draft q = (0.7, 0.3) and target p = (0.4, 0.6) over two tokens {A, B}. The draft proposes A. What is the probability A is kept, and if not, what is sampled?
options: Kept with prob 0.4; otherwise sample from p
Kept with prob 4/7; otherwise output B with probability 1
Kept with prob 0.7; otherwise output B
Always kept, since A has nonzero target probability
blocks.explain: Acceptance is min(1, p(A)/q(A)) = 0.4/0.7 = 4/7. The residual max(0, p - q) = (0, 0.3) normalizes to B with probability 1. Check: P(A) = 0.7 x 4/7 = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.3 + 0.7 x 3/7 = 0.6.

blocks.question: A teammate 'simplifies' the sampler: on rejection, sample the replacement from p instead of the residual. What happens?
options: Nothing; p and the residual are the same distribution
Outputs become biased toward tokens the draft under-proposes, because their accepted mass is counted twice
Outputs become biased toward tokens the draft over-proposes
Acceptance rate drops but outputs stay exact
blocks.explain: Rejection still happens with probability 0.3 in the toy example, but the replacement now follows p, so each token gets min(p, q) + 0.3 p(x): 0.45, 0.26, 0.16, 0.13 instead of 0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1. 'a' and 'dog', which the draft over-proposes, gain mass. The residual sends rejected mass only to under-covered tokens, adding exactly the missing p(x) - q(x).

blocks.question: Which pair of models has the higher acceptance rate beta for a single position?
options: Both are equal because both drafts put most mass on the first token
blocks.explain: beta = sum of min(p, q). First pair: 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.6. Second pair: 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9. What matters is overlap with the target, not agreeing on the top token.

lessons.title: How many tokens per round, and what speedup to expect

blocks.md: Leviathan et al. model each guess as accepted independently with probability $\alpha$ (a simplification; real acceptance varies with context). A round then keeps guesses until the first rejection, capped at $\gamma$, and always adds one target token. The number of tokens per round is a capped geometric variable.

blocks.title: Tokens produced by one round, alpha = 0.8, gamma = 4

scenes.caption: First guess rejected: probability 1 - 0.8 = 0.2, and the round still yields 1 target token.
k guesses accepted then a rejection has probability 0.8^k x 0.2: 0.16, 0.128, 0.1024 for k = 1, 2, 3.
All 4 accepted: 0.8^4 = 0.4096, giving 4 + 1 bonus = 5 tokens. The cap makes this the most likely outcome. Expected tokens: 3.36 per target pass.

blocks.caption: Leviathan et al., Equation 1. For alpha = 0.8 and gamma = 4 this is 3.36; it can never exceed 1 / (1 - alpha).

blocks.title: Expected tokens per target pass vs lookahead gamma

scenes.caption: alpha = 0.6: diminishing returns arrive fast. gamma = 2 gives 1.96 tokens, gamma = 10 only 2.49, close to the ceiling of 2.5.
alpha = 0.8: gamma = 2 gives 2.44, gamma = 5 gives 3.69 (matching Table 1 of the paper), and the ceiling is 5.
alpha = 0.9: the ceiling rises to 10 and long drafts keep paying: gamma = 10 gives 6.86 tokens per pass. Acceptance rate is the lever that matters most.

blocks.md: Tokens per pass is not yet speed, because drafting costs time. Leviathan et al. define the **cost coefficient** $c$ as the time of one draft step divided by one target step. A round costs $\gamma c + 1$ target-step units (assuming the wide verify pass costs one step), so the expected walltime improvement is:

blocks.caption: Theorem 3.8. Assumes enough spare compute to verify gamma + 1 positions in one step, and long generations.

blocks.title: Walltime speedup vs gamma for a draft costing c target steps

scenes.caption: alpha = 0.8, c = 0.05: the speedup peaks at gamma = 8 with 3.09x, then falls because each extra draft step costs more than the expected gain.
Same alpha with c = 0.128, the ratio of Chen et al.'s 1.8 ms draft to 14.1 ms target: the best gamma drops to 5 and the speedup to 2.25x.
alpha = 0.6, c = 0.05: best gamma 4, only 1.92x. A weaker draft wants shorter rounds.
alpha = 0.2, c = 0: like Leviathan's bigram drafter for translation (alpha about 0.2, free to run). gamma = 3 gives 1.25x, as the paper reports.

blocks.md: Two consequences from the paper. **Break-even**: if $\alpha > c$ some $\gamma$ gives a speedup, of at least $(1+\alpha)/(1+c)$ (Corollary 3.9). **Compute is not free**: total arithmetic grows by $(1-\alpha)(\gamma \hat{c} + \gamma + 1)/(1-\alpha^{\gamma+1})$, where $\hat c$ is the draft's arithmetic per token relative to the target. With a free draft, $\alpha = 0.8$ and $\gamma = 5$ give 3.69x speed for 1.63x the operations.

Measured numbers line up. On T5-XXL (11B) with a T5-small (77M) draft, batch 1 on a TPU v4, Leviathan et al. measured $\alpha$ = 0.75 and a 3.4x speedup for English-German translation at temperature 0, and $\alpha$ = 0.62 and 2.6x at temperature 1. Chen et al. measured 1.92x to 2.46x on Chinchilla 70B with $K = 4$. Leviathan et al. saw higher acceptance at temperature 0 than at 1, and Chen et al. saw their largest gain on code (HumanEval).

Speedup is not tokens per pass. A draft that is accurate but slow (high alpha, high c) can lose to a weaker but nearly free one. Leviathan et al. found drafts about two orders of magnitude smaller than the target usually balanced alpha and c best.

blocks.question: Your draft has alpha = 0.6 and c = 0.05. A colleague sets gamma = 10 'to get more tokens per pass'. Using the speedup formula, what happens?
options: Speedup rises to about 2.5x, the ceiling
Speedup is unchanged; gamma only affects throughput
Speedup falls to about 1.66x, below the 1.92x at gamma = 4
Decoding becomes slower than plain decoding
blocks.explain: Tokens per pass barely grow past gamma = 4 (2.31 to 2.49), but draft cost grows linearly: (1 - 0.6^11)/(0.4 x 1.5) = 1.66 versus 1.92 at gamma = 4. Still above 1, so not slower than plain decoding.

blocks.question: Which change raises the maximum achievable speedup when the draft is free (c = 0)?
options: Increasing gamma beyond 20
Lowering the target's temperature has no effect
Using a bigger GPU for the draft
Raising alpha, because the speedup is capped by 1/(1 - alpha)
blocks.explain: With c = 0 the speedup is the expected tokens per pass, bounded by 1/(1 - alpha) however large gamma gets. Only better acceptance raises the cap; lower temperature usually helps because it sharpens both distributions.

lessons.title: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees

blocks.md: A separate draft model is awkward in practice: you need one with the same tokenizer, it has its own KV cache and serving setup, and for a small target there may be no smaller sibling. **Medusa** (Cai et al., 2024) removes the draft model. It adds $K$ extra **decoding heads** on the target's last hidden state $h_t$: the original LM head predicts token $t+1$ and head $k$ predicts token $t+k+1$, all from the same forward pass.

blocks.caption: Each Medusa head is one feed-forward layer with a residual connection. W2 starts as a copy of the LM head and W1 at zero, so heads start out predicting what the base model predicts.

blocks.title: Medusa: extra heads on the frozen backbone

scenes.caption: A normal decode step: the backbone produces h_t and the LM head predicts the next token.
Medusa heads read the same h_t and guess further ahead. No extra backbone pass: drafting costs only a few small matrix multiplies.
Medusa-1 trains only the heads on a frozen backbone (5 hours for Vicuna-7B on one A100, 60k ShareGPT samples). Medusa-2 also fine-tunes the backbone with a combined loss for better heads.

blocks.md: Head $k$ is guessing a token several positions out without seeing the tokens in between, so its top-1 guess is often wrong. Medusa therefore takes the **top-$s_k$** guesses of each head and forms their Cartesian product, a **token tree**: with $s_1 = 2$ and $s_2 = 3$ there are 2 first-level nodes and $2 \times 3 = 6$ second-level nodes. In general the tree has $\sum_{k=1}^{K} \prod_{i=1}^{k} s_i$ nodes.

To verify all branches in one target pass, flatten the tree into one sequence and replace the causal mask with a **tree attention mask**: each node may attend to the cached prefix and to its own ancestors only, and its position index is its depth. This idea appears in SpecInfer (Miao et al.) and Medusa, and EAGLE uses it too.

blocks.title: Tree attention mask for 2 x 3 candidates (1 = may attend)

scenes.caption: Rows are queries, columns keys, for the 8 tree nodes after the prefix (the prefix itself is visible to all). Level 1 holds head 1's top 2 'It' and 'I'; level 2 holds head 2's top 3 under each.
'is', 'was', 'has' attend to 'It' and themselves, not to 'I' or each other. Each row is exactly the causal mask of one candidate path, so 8 positions verify 6 full paths.
'think' sees only 'I' and itself. Position ids follow depth (0 for It and I, 1 for the rest), so positional encodings match what each path would get as a plain sequence.
Without the tree, these 6 paths would need 6 sequences of length 2, i.e. 12 positions and a batch of 6. The shared first-level tokens are computed once.

blocks.md: After the pass, the engine picks the **longest accepted path**. With greedy decoding that is the deepest branch whose tokens all match the target's argmax. With sampling you need a tree version of the rejection rule. SpecInfer's multi-step speculative sampling tries a node's children one at a time: accept child $x$ with probability $\min(1, p(x)/q(x))$; on rejection, replace $p$ by $\text{norm}(\max(0, p - q))$ and try the next child; if all children fail, sample from what is left of $p$. SpecInfer proves this still yields exactly the target distribution.

Not every tree method is lossless. Medusa's optional **typical acceptance** keeps a candidate if the target's probability exceeds $\min(\epsilon, \delta e^{-H(p)})$, a threshold that depends on the entropy $H$. It raises speed at higher temperatures but no longer samples from the target's distribution. Medusa-2 also changes the backbone weights, so outputs differ from the original model.

Reported results: Medusa-1 gives over 2.2x speedup on Vicuna models without changing outputs, and Medusa-2 gives 2.3x to 2.8x (Cai et al., MT-Bench). The paper recommends training 5 heads and tuning a sparse tree; their tuned tree for Medusa-2 Vicuna-7B has 64 nodes and depth 4.

blocks.question: With s1 = 3, s2 = 2, s3 = 2, how many tree nodes must the target verify in one pass?
blocks.explain: Level sizes are 3, 3 x 2 = 6 and 3 x 2 x 2 = 12, for 3 + 6 + 12 = 21 nodes. Twelve full candidate paths share their prefixes, which is why tree attention is cheaper than 12 separate sequences of length 3.

blocks.question: A tree-attention kernel accidentally uses the ordinary causal mask on the flattened tree. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; causal masking is a superset of tree masking
Only the position ids are off by one
The pass becomes slower but results are identical
Each node also attends to earlier sibling branches, so the target scores tokens in contexts that never occur and verification becomes wrong
blocks.explain: Under a causal mask 'think' would attend to 'It', 'is', 'was' and so on, a context that is not its real prefix. Its distribution is then wrong and so are the accept and reject decisions. The mask must restrict attention to ancestors.

lessons.title: EAGLE drafts, prompt lookup, and speculation in vLLM

blocks.md: **EAGLE** (Li et al., 2024) keeps a small autoregressive drafter but feeds it the target's own **features**, the second-to-top-layer hidden states before the LM head. The drafter is one FC layer plus one transformer decoder layer, and it reuses the target's embedding and LM head. Its input is the feature sequence together with the token sequence shifted one step ahead, so it knows which token was actually sampled; the paper reports this fixes the uncertainty of predicting features alone.

The EAGLE drafter is cheap to build: 0.24B trainable parameters for a 7B target and 0.99B for 70B, trained on a fixed ShareGPT dataset in 1 to 2 days on one A100 server for the 70B models. It drafts a tree and verifies with tree attention and the lossless sampling rule, reporting 2.7x to 3.5x latency speedup for LLaMA2-Chat 70B.

**EAGLE-2** observed that the drafter is well calibrated: draft tokens with confidence below 0.05 were accepted about 4% of the time, those above 0.95 about 98%. So it grows a **dynamic tree**: the value of a node is the product of confidences along its path (an estimate that the whole path is accepted), it expands the top-k nodes per level, then reranks all nodes and keeps the top m. Reported speedups are 3.05x to 4.26x, 20% to 40% faster than EAGLE-1.

blocks.title: EAGLE-2 dynamic draft tree (example from the paper)

scenes.caption: Layer 1: the drafter proposes 'is' (confidence 0.6) and 'has' (0.2). A node's value is the product of confidences on its path.
Layer 2 values: a 0.48, the 0.06, to 0.14, a 0.02. EAGLE-2 expands only the top 2 by value, 'a' and 'to', instead of every node.
Layer 3 values: good 0.336, nice 0.048, be 0.084, do 0.028. Deeper nodes have lower values because every factor is at most 1.

Rerank: keep the 8 highest values, counting the root 'It' (value 1) as the paper's figure does. The shallow 'the' (0.06) beats the deeper 'nice' (0.048) and 'do'. A child never outranks its parent, so the kept set is a connected tree.

blocks.md: **EAGLE-3** found that adding training data helped EAGLE little, and blamed the feature-prediction loss. It drops that loss and predicts tokens directly, and instead of the top layer it concatenates **low, middle and high** layer features of the target (3 times the hidden size) and projects them back with an FC layer. Because drafted positions have no target features, training feeds the drafter its own outputs, a technique the authors call **training-time test**. The paper reports up to 6.5x speedup, about 1.4x over EAGLE-2, and 1.38x throughput at batch size 64 in SGLang.

The cheapest drafter is no model at all. **Prompt lookup decoding** (an n-gram drafter) takes the last few generated tokens, searches for the same n-gram earlier in the prompt or output, and proposes the tokens that followed it. Its cost ratio $c$ is essentially 0, so speedup is just tokens per pass. It shines when outputs copy the input: summarization, document QA, code edits.

scenes.caption: The generated text ends with 'total cost of'. Take this 3-token suffix as the search key.
An earlier occurrence sits at positions 0 to 2. No model ran; this is a string search over token ids.
Copy the 4 tokens that followed the match as draft guesses. The target verifies them exactly as it would a model's guesses, so a wrong copy costs one round but never changes the output.

blocks.md: The prompt-lookup reference implementation reports about 2.4x average speedup on summarization and context QA with Mistral-7B-Instruct at greedy decoding on one A100, and much less on open-ended chat with short prompts. It ships in Hugging Face transformers as `prompt_lookup_num_tokens` and in vLLM as the `ngram` method.

In vLLM you enable speculation with a `speculative_config`. The docs list model-based methods (EAGLE, MTP heads, a separate draft model, PARD) and model-free ones (n-gram, suffix decoding). The examples below follow the vLLM docs; check them for current options and supported model pairs.

blocks.code:
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

# EAGLE-3 draft head (example from the vLLM docs)
llm = LLM(
    model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct",
    tensor_parallel_size=2,
    speculative_config={
        "model": "RedHatAI/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-speculator.eagle3",
        "draft_tensor_parallel_size": 2,
        "num_speculative_tokens": 2,
        "method": "eagle3",
    },
)

# Draft-free alternative: prompt lookup (n-gram)
llm_ngram = LLM(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    speculative_config={
        "method": "ngram",
        "num_speculative_tokens": 5,
        "prompt_lookup_max": 4,
    },
)
out = llm.generate(["Summarize: ..."], SamplingParams(temperature=0.8))
blocks.caption: num_speculative_tokens is gamma. The draft head is trained for a specific target model family; the vLLM EAGLE page lists pre-trained heads for common targets.

blocks.md: When does it pay off? The vLLM docs say speculative decoding reduces inter-token latency for **medium-to-low QPS, memory-bound** workloads. At high load the batch already keeps the GPU busy with useful arithmetic, so the extra verification work (lesson 4: 1.63x the operations at alpha 0.8, gamma 5) competes with other requests instead of filling idle cycles.

vLLM documents its rejection sampler as lossless up to hardware numerics, tested with convergence and greedy-equality tests, while noting that batch size changes can shift logprobs. Its FLy verification mode is explicitly not distribution preserving, like Medusa's typical acceptance.

All variants share one loop: draft cheaply (small model, extra heads, feature-level head, or string lookup), verify a chain or tree in one target pass, keep the accepted prefix plus one target token. They differ only in how they guess, and that sets alpha and c.

blocks.question: A service runs a 70B chat model at very high request rate with large batches and the GPUs are compute bound. Would enabling EAGLE likely cut cost per token?
options: Yes, speculation always reduces work per token
Probably not: the batch already uses the compute, and rejected draft tokens add verification work that competes with other requests
Yes, because EAGLE heads replace the target's LM head
No, because EAGLE cannot run with batch sizes above 1
blocks.explain: Speculation turns idle compute into fewer sequential steps. When the GPU is already compute bound, wasted verification is real cost. vLLM documents the biggest gains at medium-to-low QPS; EAGLE-3 still reports some throughput gain at batch 64 in SGLang, so measure your workload.

blocks.question: Which drafter fits best for an assistant that rewrites long user-provided code files with small edits, given no budget to train anything?
options: Prompt lookup (n-gram) drafting
A freshly trained EAGLE-3 head
Medusa-2 with a fine-tuned backbone
Typical acceptance with a high threshold
blocks.explain: The output copies long spans of the input, which is exactly what n-gram lookup predicts, and it needs no training and costs almost nothing per guess (c near 0). Medusa-2 and typical acceptance also change outputs.

blocks.question: Medusa's typical acceptance, Medusa-2, EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup: which of these can change the output distribution compared to the original target model?
options: Only EAGLE-2
Typical acceptance and Medusa-2
Prompt lookup, because copied tokens skip the target
All four
blocks.explain: Typical acceptance replaces rejection sampling with a threshold, and Medusa-2 fine-tunes the backbone itself. EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup only change how drafts are proposed; verification with the standard rule keeps the target's distribution.
